findings.issue_text: Refresh-token corruption via literal fallback in `parseRefreshTokenResponse` overwrites the real token with the literal string `"refresh_token"`, permanently locking users out.
`refreshOAuthTokens` returns a raw `fetch` Response instead of adapter-specific objects, causing TypeErrors in Google, Hubspot, Zoho-bigin, and Zohocrm adapters.
Zoho-bigin passes the credential id as `userId` to `refreshOAuthTokens`, causing the sync endpoint to look up the wrong user and return mismatched credentials.
Salesforce eager refresh runs unconditionally on every `SalesforceCalendarService` instantiation without a feature flag, forcing synchronous token refresh and DB write.
Salesforce eager refresh success check uses `if (response.statusText !== "OK")`, which is unreliable in HTTP/2 and can reject legitimate 200 responses.
Salesforce refresh uses `salesforceTokenSchema` requiring `scope` and `signature`, which are occasionally omitted, causing `parseRefreshTokenResponse` to throw.
Salesforce refreshed `access_token` is computed and stored but not used, as a fresh `jsforce.Connection` is constructed with the old `refresh_token`.
`minimumTokenResponseSchema` computed keys evaluate to `"[object Object]"`, so the schema effectively only requires `access_token` and accepts malformed token responses.
Webhook handler in `app-credential.ts` lacks a try/catch around `JSON.parse` and `symmetricDecrypt`, leaking stack details on bad input.
Webhook handler passes `""` as the AES key when `CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY` is unset, causing `symmetricDecrypt` to throw.
Webhook handler in `app-credential.ts` is missing an HTTP-method check, allowing GET requests which throw on `parse(req.body)`.
Office365 error behavior changed from logging and continuing to throwing on `parseRefreshTokenResponse` failure, crashing calendar operations on transient non-conformant responses.

Google CalendarService stores the wrong credential shape because parseRefreshTokenResponse returns the full Zod safeParse result ({ success, data }) instead of just the parsed data, corrupting stored OAuth credentials on every refresh
refreshOAuthTokens returns a raw Response object in sharing mode but all callers expect parsed JSON, breaking token refresh for every integration when credential sharing is enabled

No authentication (shared secret, signature, or auth header) on outbound requests to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT, allowing anyone with the endpoint URL and calcomUserId to trigger token-refresh lookups and obtain live access tokens

minimumTokenResponseSchema has nonsense computed keys (z.string().toString()) that don't produce meaningful property names, so the schema only validates access_token: string and barely validates responses
parseRefreshTokenResponse stores the literal string "refresh_token" whenever the refresh_token field is missing, persisting bogus values to the DB and corrupting credentials
Webhook secret compared with non-constant-time !== instead of crypto.timingSafeEqual, risking timing side channels that could leak the webhook secret
.env.example suggests openssl rand -base64 24 for CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY but docs require 32 bytes, causing self-hosters to configure an invalid AES key
Webhook handler does not enforce HTTP method (no req.method === "POST" check), allowing any verb that supplies the secret and body to create/update credentials
Salesforce uses response.statusText !== "OK" for success check, which is locale/implementation-dependent and may spuriously throw HttpError 400 on valid responses
Unhandled JSON.parse / decrypt failures in webhook handler can throw unhandled exceptions (500) on malformed ciphertext or JSON, leaking stack traces

parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts: Broken Zod schema where computed keys [z.string().toString()] collapse to '[object Object]', causing Zod to strip unknown fields and write literal string 'refresh_token' into credentials

Google Calendar CalendarService.ts: res?.data is undefined when credential sharing is enabled because refreshOAuthTokens returns a fetch Response instead of the Google OAuth library's { res: { data } } wrapper, causing a TypeError

Hubspot CalendarService.ts: refreshOAuthTokens returns a fetch Response instead of HubspotToken when sharing is enabled, causing downstream code to access undefined fields and persist corrupted credentials

Zoho CRM CalendarService.ts: Type mismatch where refreshOAuthTokens returns a fetch Response instead of AxiosResponse when sharing is enabled, causing zohoCrmTokenInfo.data to be undefined and throwing a TypeError

Zoho Bigin CalendarService.ts: Same type mismatch as Zoho CRM where refreshOAuthTokens returns a fetch Response instead of AxiosResponse when sharing is enabled, causing tokenInfo.data to be undefined and crashing

Salesforce CalendarService.ts: Broken minimumTokenResponseSchema strips essential token fields (instance_url, signature, id, scope, token_type) required by salesforceTokenSchema when sharing is enabled, causing jsforce.Connection to fail

refreshOAuthTokens.ts: Lacks timeout, retry, response status check, and error handling for the sync endpoint fetch call, which can cause indefinite hangs and undefined behavior downstream on non-2xx responses
`minimumTokenResponseSchema` uses `.toString()` on Zod schemas resulting in literal string keys like "[object Object]", causing `safeParse` to always fail and breaking the credential-sync feature
`refresh_token` is overwritten with the literal string "refresh_token" when missing from the response, persisting an invalid value that breaks future refresh attempts
`parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the full `SafeParseReturnType` object instead of just `data`, changing the shape of persisted credentials and breaking Google Calendar refresh
`refreshOAuthTokens` returns a fetch `Response` instead of the expected parsed data shape when sync is active, breaking OAuth refresh for Google, Hubspot, Zoho Bigin, and Zoho CRM
Salesforce refresh bypasses `refreshOAuthTokens` and calls `fetch` directly, breaking credential-sync feature consistency when enabled
Salesforce uses `response.statusText !== "OK"` for success check, which is unreliable and empty for HTTP/2
Dead code `if (!accessTokenParsed.success)` in Salesforce refresh path is unreachable because `parseRefreshTokenResponse` already throws on failure
`appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` throws an unhandled `ZodError` resulting in a 500 response instead of 400/422 for malformed input
Missing `req.method` check in the `app-credential` webhook route allows processing of non-POST requests like GET/PUT
Non-constant-time string comparison for webhook secret (`!==`) enables timing side-channel attacks on the credential-write endpoint
parseRefreshTokenResponse returns the safeParse result object instead of the parsed data, causing the stored credential to be corrupted and breaking subsequent refresh/API calls
parseRefreshTokenResponse overwrites a missing refresh_token with the literal string "refresh_token", which bricks credentials on the next refresh cycle
minimumTokenResponseSchema uses computed keys z.string().toString() which evaluate to "[object Object]", causing schema validation to be malformed and ineffective
Google refresh path crashes when credential sharing is enabled because refreshOAuthTokens returns a fetch Response and token.access_token throws a TypeError
refreshOAuthTokens has no timeout, retry, or response.ok check on the credential-sync fetch, leading to hung requests or malformed token objects being persisted
Zoho Bigin refresh path passes credentialId instead of credential.userId as the userId to the sync endpoint, resulting in the wrong or no tokens being returned
Salesforce error check uses response.statusText which is unreliable in HTTP/2 and can cause successful responses to trip the error check
Salesforce refresh path bypasses refreshOAuthTokens and persists locally, breaking credential-sharing mode for self-hosters
Webhook handler for app-credential has no HTTP method guard, allowing GET, DELETE, or PUT requests to create/update credentials
Webhook secret is compared with === instead of constant-time comparison, exposing a timing-attack surface
Uncaught throws from zod.parse, JSON.parse, and symmetricDecrypt in the webhook handler produce 500 errors with stack traces instead of clean 400 responses
symmetricDecrypt uses an empty-string fallback for the AES key if the env var is unset, silently proceeding with decryption instead of failing fast
Office365video VideoApiAdapter passes "msteams" as the appSlug to refreshOAuthTokens instead of "office365video", preventing the parent app from matching the credential
Lark CalendarService runs handleLarkError against the sync endpoint's raw fetch Response, causing mis-parsing or masking the real failure if the error shape differs
APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED evaluates to a string or undefined instead of a boolean, causing unexpected behavior in strict equality or serialization checks

Broken Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts:8-13 where computed property keys [z.string().toString()] evaluate to '[object Object]', causing the second key to overwrite the first and resulting in a schema that doesn't check for expiry or allow additional properties

In parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts:24-26, refresh_token is set to the literal string 'refresh_token' instead of preserving the existing token or omitting the field, causing subsequent refresh calls to fail with invalid grant

Return type boundary leak in refreshOAuthTokens.ts:6-19 where the sync path returns a fetch Response object but axios-based callers (Google, Hubspot, Zoho Bigin, Zoho CRM) expect axios response shapes with .data properties, causing runtime failures when credential sharing is enabled

Salesforce token refresh in CalendarService.ts:75-98 is not wrapped in refreshOAuthTokens and always refreshes on every service construction, bypassing the sync endpoint when credential sharing is enabled and making unnecessary network calls
Webhook handler in app-credential.ts:38-39 has no HTTP method guard, accepting any method (GET, DELETE, etc.) which causes unhandled Zod parse errors on requests with no body

Unguarded JSON.parse on decrypted payload in app-credential.ts:62-63 can throw unhandled 500 errors if decryption produces non-JSON output, and the || '' fallback for CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY masks misconfiguration instead of failing fast

Header lookup in app-credential.ts:47-50 is case-sensitive but Node.js normalizes header names to lowercase, so if CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME is set with uppercase letters the bracket lookup will miss the header and return 403

Unreliable status check via response.statusText in Salesforce CalendarService.ts:91 which can vary by server, incorrectly rejecting valid responses with non-'OK' status text instead of using response.ok or response.status === 200

Dead code in Salesforce CalendarService.ts:95-97 where the success check after parseRefreshTokenResponse is unreachable because parseRefreshTokenResponse throws on failure rather than returning a result with .success === false

parseRefreshTokenResponse returns the full SafeParseReturnType including .success and .error wrapper fields rather than just parsed data, causing callers like Google CalendarService.ts:89 to use the wrapper object directly as the credential key
refresh_token is silently overwritten with the literal string 'refresh_token' when the sync endpoint doesn't return it, corrupting persisted credentials and causing permanent refresh failures
refreshOAuthTokens returns a raw fetch Response for the sync path but callers expect different object shapes, causing crashes in Google, Hubspot, Zoho Bigin, and Zoho CRM integrations
credentialId variable may be undefined in Zoho Bigin CalendarService.ts:91, causing a ReferenceError even when credential sharing is disabled
Webhook endpoint trusts userId from request body with no per-user authorization, allowing anyone with the webhook secret to overwrite arbitrary users' credentials
Webhook secret comparison uses non-constant-time (!==) operator, enabling timing side-channel attacks to recover the secret
TOCTOU race condition in webhook credential upsert uses findFirst then create/update instead of prisma upsert, allowing duplicate credentials
Salesforce token refresh check uses fragile response.statusText !== 'OK' which can fail with HTTP/2 or proxies; should use response.ok or response.status === 200
minimumTokenResponseSchema uses z.string().toString() as computed keys, which resolve to '[object Object]' — schema works by accident and is a maintenance hazard
Salesforce code unconditionally refreshes tokens on every service instantiation instead of lazily, causing unnecessary API calls and DB writes on every calendar operation
Webhook uses z.parse() instead of safeParse(), throwing unhandled ZodError on malformed input resulting in 500 errors; also no HTTP method check causes GET to 500
Webhook stores decrypted credential keys directly, potentially bypassing at-rest encryption if encryption is applied at the application layer rather than Prisma middleware

goldens.comment: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.

The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.

parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse result ({ success, data, error }), not the credential key object. Persisting that as key stores the wrapper instead of the token payload; we should store the parsed data or use schema parse.

When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, the refreshFunction helper returns the fetch Response, but several callers (for example GoogleCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting res.data, and HubspotCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting a HubspotToken) assume it returns the integration-specific token object. That mismatch will cause runtime errors in the sync-enabled path unless the return type or those call sites are adjusted.

When the sync endpoint path is used, res is a fetch Response and has no .data; res?.data will be undefined and token.access_token will throw at runtime. This relies on a consistent return shape from refreshOAuthTokens, which isn’t guaranteed currently.

The `refreshOAuthTokens` function is passed `credentialId` instead of `userId`, which breaks the credential sync functionality by causing incorrect user lookups. This issue can lead to failures in syncing user credentials, impacting user experience.

The Salesforce integration checks `response.statusText` instead of `response.ok` when handling OAuth token refresh responses. This can lead to unreliable behavior, as a successful response may not be correctly identified, resulting in the use of stale credentials and potential authentication failures.

The `jsforce.Connection` is created using stale `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url` after a token refresh, which can lead to authentication failures and incorrect data access. Ensure that the connection is established using the refreshed token values instead.

The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Salesforce eager refresh runs unconditionally on every `SalesforceCalendarService` instantiation without a feature flag, forcing synchronous token refresh and DB write.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does not show any code in `SalesforceCalendarService` that performs an eager/unconditional token refresh during instantiation, nor any synchronous refresh/DB write logic tied to the constructor. The shown changes are limited to adding `zod`, importing `parseRefreshTokenResponse`, and defining a `salesforceTokenSchema`; no feature-flag checks or refresh calls are present in the provided Salesforce snippet. The finding asserts behavior that is not verifiable from this diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Salesforce eager refresh success check uses `if (response.statusText !== "OK")`, which is unreliable in HTTP/2 and can reject legitimate 200 responses.

adjudication.rationale: The diff only shows the introduction of `salesforceTokenSchema` (with required `scope`/`signature`) and an import of `parseRefreshTokenResponse` in `SalesforceCalendarService.ts`. It does not show any refresh-token code path using `salesforceTokenSchema` with `parseRefreshTokenResponse`, nor any actual parsing/validation of a refresh response. The claim that Salesforce refresh responses “occasionally omit” `scope`/`signature` is also external/behavioral and not verifiable from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Salesforce refreshed `access_token` is computed and stored but not used, as a fresh `jsforce.Connection` is constructed with the old `refresh_token`.

adjudication.rationale: The diff snippet for `packages/app-store/salesforce/lib/CalendarService.ts` only shows new imports (`z`, `parseRefreshTokenResponse`) and the introduction of `salesforceTokenSchema`, then truncates before any token refresh logic or `jsforce.Connection` construction is shown. There is no verifiable evidence in the provided diff that a refreshed `access_token` is stored but unused, or that a new `jsforce.Connection` is constructed with an old `refresh_token`. This finding depends on code not included in the diff excerpt, so it cannot be confirmed from what’s shown.

adjudication_records.issue_text: `minimumTokenResponseSchema` computed keys evaluate to `"[object Object]"`, so the schema effectively only requires `access_token` and accepts malformed token responses.
Webhook handler in `app-credential.ts` lacks a try/catch around `JSON.parse` and `symmetricDecrypt`, leaking stack details on bad input.
Webhook handler passes `""` as the AES key when `CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY` is unset, causing `symmetricDecrypt` to throw.

adjudication.rationale:
In the new webhook handler, decryption is performed as:

```ts
symmetricDecrypt(reqBody.keys, process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY || "")
```

So when `CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY` is unset, an empty string is passed as the AES key. There is no validation/early return for a missing key and no try/catch around `symmetricDecrypt` or the subsequent `JSON.parse(...)`. With an empty/invalid key, decryption will fail in some way (either `symmetricDecrypt` throws or returns non-JSON), which will raise an exception and result in an unhandled 500 for the webhook request. The exact throw location depends on `symmetricDecrypt` implementation, but the diff verifiably introduces the bad default and lack of error handling.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Webhook handler in `app-credential.ts` is missing an HTTP-method check, allowing GET requests which throw on `parse(req.body)`.

adjudication.rationale: The new Next.js API route `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts` exports a `handler` that performs auth checks and then unconditionally executes `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` without checking `req.method`. Next.js API routes can be invoked with GET (and other methods); for GET requests `req.body` will typically be `undefined`/empty, causing Zod `.parse` to throw and result in a 500 rather than a controlled 405/400 response. This is a verifiable defect introduced by the diff (missing HTTP method guard).

adjudication_records.issue_text: Office365 error behavior changed from logging and continuing to throwing on `parseRefreshTokenResponse` failure, crashing calendar operations on transient non-conformant responses.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does change Office365 token-refresh handling: it replaces `refreshTokenResponseSchema.safeParse(...)` plus `console.error(...)` (and then continuing) with `parseRefreshTokenResponse(...)`, which throws if validation fails. That behavioral change is verifiable. However, the finding’s claim that this is a *defect* (“crashing calendar operations on transient non-conformant responses”) is not verifiable from the diff: it assumes such transient schema mismatches occur and that the thrown error is not handled upstream. The change could also be an intentional correctness hardening to fail fast on invalid token responses rather than silently proceeding with stale credentials.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Google CalendarService stores the wrong credential shape because parseRefreshTokenResponse returns the full Zod safeParse result ({ success, data }) instead of just the parsed data, corrupting stored OAuth credentials on every refresh
refreshOAuthTokens returns a raw Response object in sharing mode but all callers expect parsed JSON, breaking token refresh for every integration when credential sharing is enabled

No authentication (shared secret, signature, or auth header) on outbound requests to CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT, allowing anyone with the endpoint URL and calcomUserId to trigger token-refresh lookups and obtain live access tokens

adjudication.rationale: The new helper `refreshOAuthTokens` sends a POST to `process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` with only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` in the body (via `new URLSearchParams(...)`) and does not include any authentication material (no shared-secret header, signature/HMAC, Authorization header, etc.). This is directly verifiable in the diff. As a result, the receiving credential-sync service has no built-in way to distinguish legitimate Cal.com calls from arbitrary third-party requests that know/guess the URL and userId/appSlug, matching the finding’s core claim (lack of auth on outbound sync requests).

adjudication_records.issue_text: minimumTokenResponseSchema has nonsense computed keys (z.string().toString()) that don't produce meaningful property names, so the schema only validates access_token: string and barely validates responses
parseRefreshTokenResponse stores the literal string "refresh_token" whenever the refresh_token field is missing, persisting bogus values to the DB and corrupting credentials
Webhook secret compared with non-constant-time !== instead of crypto.timingSafeEqual, risking timing side channels that could leak the webhook secret

adjudication.rationale:
In the newly added API route `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts`, the webhook secret is validated via a direct inequality check:

```ts
if (req.headers[process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME || "calcom-webhook-secret"] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET)
```

This is a regular string/primitive comparison and is not constant-time. For secret validation, this can theoretically leak information via timing differences (early-exit comparisons), which is why `crypto.timingSafeEqual` (with proper normalization to buffers and length checks) is typically recommended for shared-secret comparisons. This behavior is present in the diff and is directly verifiable in the added code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: .env.example suggests openssl rand -base64 24 for CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY but docs require 32 bytes, causing self-hosters to configure an invalid AES key

adjudication.rationale: In `.env.example`, the new `CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY` section states the key "must be 32 bytes for AES256 encryption algorithm" but then recommends generating it with `openssl rand -base64 24`. `openssl rand -base64 24` generates 24 random bytes (then base64-encodes them), not 32 bytes of key material, so the guidance is internally inconsistent and can lead self-hosters to configure a key that does not meet the stated 32-byte requirement.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Webhook handler does not enforce HTTP method (no req.method === "POST" check), allowing any verb that supplies the secret and body to create/update credentials

adjudication.rationale: In the newly added `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts` handler, there is no `req.method` check (e.g., rejecting non-POST requests with 405). The code will proceed for any HTTP verb as long as the caller supplies the expected header secret and a body that satisfies the Zod schema, and will then create/update credentials via Prisma. So the finding is directly verifiable in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Salesforce uses response.statusText !== "OK" for success check, which is locale/implementation-dependent and may spuriously throw HttpError 400 on valid responses

adjudication.rationale: The provided diff does not show any Salesforce code that checks `response.statusText !== "OK"` or throws an `HttpError 400` based on `statusText`. The Salesforce changes visible here are limited to adding a `zod` import, adding `parseRefreshTokenResponse` import, and defining a `salesforceTokenSchema`; the relevant success-check logic is not present in the shown hunks. Therefore the finding cannot be verified as a real issue in this diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Unhandled JSON.parse / decrypt failures in webhook handler can throw unhandled exceptions (500) on malformed ciphertext or JSON, leaking stack traces

parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts: Broken Zod schema where computed keys [z.string().toString()] collapse to '[object Object]', causing Zod to strip unknown fields and write literal string 'refresh_token' into credentials

adjudication.rationale: Yes. In `parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts`, the `minimumTokenResponseSchema` uses computed keys like `[z.string().toString()]`. `z.string()` returns a Zod schema object, and calling `.toString()` on it produces a constant string (typically `"[object Object]"`), not a dynamic key matcher. Both computed keys also likely collide to the same literal key, overwriting one another. As a result, the schema does not accept real token fields like `expiry_date` or `refresh_token`, and because `z.object(...)` strips unknown keys by default, `safeParse(response)` will drop those fields. The subsequent code then sees `refresh_token` missing and sets it to the literal string `"refresh_token"`, which can then be written into credentials.

In `packages/app-store/googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts`, the new code assigns `const res = await refreshOAuthTokens(...)` and then does `const token = res?.data; googleCredentials.access_token = token.access_token;`.

But `refreshOAuthTokens` (new file) returns two different shapes:

- credential-sharing path: returns the result of `fetch(process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT, ...)`, i.e. a standard Fetch `Response` object, which does not have `.data`

The diff does not show Zoho integrations using `refreshOAuthTokens`, so that portion of the finding isn’t directly verifiable here, but the core shape-mismatch bug is clearly introduced and will break at least Google and Hubspot when the sync path is active.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Webhook endpoint trusts userId from request body with no per-user authorization, allowing anyone with the webhook secret to overwrite arbitrary users' credentials

adjudication.rationale: The newly added API route `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts` authenticates requests solely by comparing a shared secret in a header (`req.headers[CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME]`) to `process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`. After that check, it directly uses `userId` from the request body (`reqBody.userId`) to look up/create/update `prisma.credential` for that user (`where: { userId: reqBody.userId, appId: appMetadata.slug }`) with no additional per-user authorization or binding between the caller and that user. Therefore, any caller who knows the webhook secret can supply an arbitrary `userId` and overwrite/create credentials for that user.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Webhook secret comparison uses non-constant-time (!==) operator, enabling timing side-channel attacks to recover the secret

adjudication.rationale:
In the new `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts` handler, the webhook secret is validated via a direct inequality check:

```ts
if (req.headers[... ] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET) {
  return res.status(403)...
}
```

This uses normal JS string comparison (`!==`), which is not constant-time and can short-circuit based on the first differing character. That creates a plausible timing side-channel for an attacker who can send many requests and measure response times to incrementally guess the secret. A constant-time comparison (e.g., `crypto.timingSafeEqual` over buffers of equal length) would avoid this class of leak.

adjudication_records.issue_text: TOCTOU race condition in webhook credential upsert uses findFirst then create/update instead of prisma upsert, allowing duplicate credentials

adjudication.rationale: In the new webhook handler, the code does a non-atomic read-then-write: `findFirst({ where: { userId, appId } })` followed by either `credential.update({ where: { id } })` or `credential.create({ data: { userId, appId, ... } })`. Under concurrent requests for the same `(userId, appId)`, both can observe “no credential” and both execute `create`, which can result in duplicate rows if the DB does not enforce a unique constraint (or a unique-constraint violation/500 if it does). This TOCTOU pattern is present in the diff and Prisma `upsert` (with a unique key) would avoid it.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Salesforce token refresh check uses fragile response.statusText !== 'OK' which can fail with HTTP/2 or proxies; should use response.ok or response.status === 200
matched_golden_ids: The Salesforce integration checks `response.statusText` instead of `response.ok` when handling OAuth token refresh responses. This can lead to unreliable behavior, as a successful response may not be correctly identified, resulting in the use of stale credentials and potential authentication failures.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate flags the same core bug: the OAuth token refresh logic relies on `response.statusText` (e.g., comparing to 'OK') rather than a reliable success indicator like `response.ok`/status code, which can misclassify successful responses and lead to stale credentials/auth failures.

adjudication_records.issue_text: minimumTokenResponseSchema uses z.string().toString() as computed keys, which resolve to '[object Object]' — schema works by accident and is a maintenance hazard

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts`, `minimumTokenResponseSchema` is defined as `z.object({ access_token: z.string(), [z.string().toString()]: z.number(), [z.string().optional().toString()]: z.unknown().optional() })`. In a JS object literal, those computed property expressions are evaluated immediately to a single string key (e.g., `"[object Object]"` or another fixed string), not a wildcard for “any string key”. That makes the schema require a property with that exact name to exist and be a number, which normal OAuth token responses will not have. Therefore `safeParse(response)` will typically fail and the code will throw `Invalid refreshed tokens were returned` when credential sharing is enabled, so this is a real correctness bug introduced by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Salesforce code unconditionally refreshes tokens on every service instantiation instead of lazily, causing unnecessary API calls and DB writes on every calendar operation

adjudication.rationale: The provided diff excerpt for `packages/app-store/salesforce/lib/CalendarService.ts` only shows new imports (`z`, `parseRefreshTokenResponse`) and the addition of a `salesforceTokenSchema`, but it does not show any token refresh logic (e.g., calling a refresh endpoint, updating credentials in Prisma) nor where/when the service instantiation occurs. Since the diff does not contain the alleged behavior (unconditional refresh on instantiation) or any new code that would cause it, the finding is not verifiable from this diff and appears to be speculation about code not shown.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Webhook uses z.parse() instead of safeParse(), throwing unhandled ZodError on malformed input resulting in 500 errors; also no HTTP method check causes GET to 500

adjudication.rationale:
In the newly added API route `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts`, the request body is validated with `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)`. `parse()` throws a `ZodError` on malformed/missing input and there is no `try/catch` (nor error middleware shown) to convert that into a 4xx response, so an invalid body can result in an unhandled exception and a 500.

Additionally, the handler does not check `req.method`. If the secret check passes (e.g., caller sends the correct header, or `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` is unset so `undefined !== undefined` is false), a GET request will proceed to `parse(req.body)` where `req.body` is typically empty/undefined, causing the same unhandled Zod error and 500. Thus both parts describe real issues present in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Webhook stores decrypted credential keys directly, potentially bypassing at-rest encryption if encryption is applied at the application layer rather than Prisma middleware

adjudication.rationale: In the new `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts` handler, the code decrypts `reqBody.keys` via `symmetricDecrypt(...)`, `JSON.parse`s it, and writes the resulting object directly into `prisma.credential.update/create` as `key: keys`. However, the finding claims this “bypasses at-rest encryption” that may exist at the application layer rather than Prisma middleware. The diff does not show any existing at-rest encryption mechanism, nor any expectation that `credential.key` must be stored encrypted. Therefore the “bypass” aspect is speculative and not verifiable from this diff alone.
